newsitem.title: USA: Twin storms slam central U.S.
newsitem.headline: Twin storms slam central U.S.

text.p: Twin storms converged on the nation's midsection Thursday, one soaking the waterlogged Ohio River Valley with rain and the other dumping another dose of winter on the northern tier of states.
Up to three inches of rain were forecast for the western end of the Ohio River Valley, endangering earthen levees holding back the cresting river in western Kentucky and southern Illinois.

"We're just waiting to see if this heavy rain comes," Coast Guard Lt. Mark Emmons said. Flash flood watches were issued for the already soaked region that included parts of Tennessee, Kentucky and Illinois.

Downstream from Paducah in Smithland, Ky., much of the sandbagging operation was completed in a drizzle as residents raised the floodwall a few feet to prepare for the Ohio River's crest Thursday at 52 feet. Some families have already left tiny Smithland, which has historic buildings dating to the 19th century.

Meanwhile, a separate storm system dumped several inches of snow on parts of North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Iowa. Sleet made for hazardous driving across northern Iowa, while Wisconsin was coated with a layer of heavy, wet snow.
The two systems, driven by winds that should bring a blast of cold air in behind the precipitation, were merging and should hit the East Coast Friday, forecasters said.
The new rain threatened weary residents of the Ohio Valley still cleaning up from the flash floods that swamped thousands of homes and lifted the Ohio River to its highest level since 1964.

The weekend tornadoes and flooding caused 59 deaths across eight states and several people were still listed as missing. The cleanup of mud and debris left behind by the floodwaters has been under way for a week in hard-hit communities in Ohio, Kentucky, West Virginia and Indiana.

High water from the Ohio River, which flows into the Mississippi River at Cairo, Ill., was expected to swell the lower Mississippi to its highest level in more than two decades, officials in Memphis, Tenn., said.

There was little or no threat of the river flooding Memphis, where a precautionary sandbag wall plugged a gap in the city's flood wall near the Pyramid, a sports arena. Overflow from the river, which was expected to crest in a week at eight feet above flood stage, already was lapping at levees set back a mile or so on the opposite side in Arkansas.
"When you get to Cairo it's like a garden hose opening up into a bathtub. The problem is, the bathtub is pretty full right now," U.S. Army Corps of Engineers spokesman Jim Pogue said.
